chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, who said: I heard Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying:
It is disliked to recite poetry for the fasting person, for the one in ihram, in the sanctuary (Mecca), on Friday, and to be recited at night.
I asked: Even if it is true poetry? He said: Even if it is true poetry.

key_terms.لِلْمُحْرِمِ: For the one in ihram (pilgrimal state)

ai.seo_question: What are the specific contexts in which reciting poetry is considered disliked in Shia jurisprudence according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) extends the concept of *makruh* (disliked) to the recitation of poetry during fasting, pilgrimage, in the Haram, on Fridays, and at night, emphasizing that this applies even to 'true' poetry. This highlights the Shia scholarly view that the aesthetic or rhetorical quality of poetry does not exempt it from ritual decorum, as excessive verbal expression may distract from spiritual presence (*khushu*) and the solemnity of these sacred times. The inclusion of 'night' suggests a concern for disrupting the tranquility of worship or sleep, aligning with broader ethical guidelines on speech in Islam.
